# Quick start {#sec-quick-start}

This chapter takes one lidar tile, `my_tile.laz`, from raw points to a
ground surface, a canopy height model, a grid of forest metrics, and a
list of tree tops, in four commands. The commands are written for the
Windows Command Prompt and assume the tools are on your `PATH`
(@sec-installing). Cell sizes are in the point cloud's own horizontal
units, feet for the tile used in this manual.

Create the output folder first. Not every tool creates a missing output
folder, and some report success without writing anything when the folder
does not exist.

```bat
mkdir out
```

## Build the ground surface

```bat
groundfilter my_tile.laz /output-raster:out/ground.tif /cellsize:5
```

`groundfilter` finds the points that hit the ground and turns them into a
ground elevation raster (a digital elevation model, or DEM) with 5 ft
cells. The tools that follow use it to turn each point's elevation into a
height above ground (@sec-groundfilter).

## Build the canopy height model

```bat
canopymodel my_tile.laz /ground:out/ground.tif /cellsize:3 /output:out/chm.tif
```

`canopymodel` keeps the highest point in each 3 ft cell and subtracts the
ground elevation beneath it, giving a canopy height model (CHM): a raster
of vegetation height (@sec-canopymodel).

## Compute gridded forest metrics

```bat
gridmetrics my_tile.laz out/ground.tif /cellsize:10 /outdir:out
```

`gridmetrics` computes height percentiles, canopy cover, height
variability, intensity statistics, and more for every 10 ft cell, and
writes them as bands of one GeoTIFF, `out/my_tile_gridmetrics.tif`
(@sec-gridmetrics). The ground surface can be given as the second
positional argument, as here, or with `/ground:`.

## Find tree tops

```bat
canopymaxima out/chm.tif /output:out/tree_tops.csv /minht:2
```

`canopymaxima` finds local height peaks on the canopy height model and
writes one row per tree top, with its location, height, and an estimated
crown diameter (@sec-canopymaxima). `/minht:2` ignores peaks lower than
2 ft.
